headlines.article_text: Meta (META) Q3 2026 earnings report: Live updates Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg demonstrates Muse, Meta's artificial intelligence agent, during the Meta Connect event in Menlo Park, California, Sept. 23, 2026. Minh Connors | Bloomberg | Getty Images Meta is slated to report third-quarter earnings after the bell on Wednesday, and investors will be looking for signs that the company's latest artificial intelligence efforts will bolster future sales. Here's what analysts polled by LSEG are expecting: Earnings per share : $5.75 Revenue : $63.2 billion It's been a big quarter for Mark Zuckerberg's company due to the initial success of the Muse AI personal assistant tool that debuted in September and shot to the top of Apple's iOS app store. That AI momentum helped Meta end September with its best month on Wall Street since 2022. Meta isn't the first to create a digital assistant that can organize people's email and scan the web for headphone deals, but the company's empire, which includes Facebook and Instagram, has helped introduce AI agents to the masses. At the same time, Meta and its AI chief Alexandr Wang have continued rolling out new foundation models and related updates at a speedy clip, including Muse Wonder , which was released last Monday. Wall Street will likely be monitoring for whether Meta plans to increase its data center-related capital expenditures, or capex, to further develop the underlying computing infrastructure needed to power AI agents and foundation models. The company revealed in July during its second-quarter earnings that it narrowed its 2026 capex guidance to come in between $130 billion and $145 billion, representing a $5 billion increase to the low end of its prior range. All that spending resulted in Meta's free cash flow in the period shrinking to $784 million from $8.55 billion in the same quarter a year earlier. Analysts expect Meta's capex to swell to $196.3 billion in 2027, according to FactSet. Meta's third-quarter daily active people, or DAP, is expected to come in at 3.65 billion, according to StreetAccount, almost flat from the prior quarter. That figure represents all of Meta's users across its family of apps like Facebook and Instagram. Meta stock chart Read more CNBC tech news Meta earnings updates: AI spending, ad revenue and stock reaction Tesla earnings loom after Musk calls SpaceX merger a 'good idea' Intel hits construction milestone at Ohio chip fab that's at least 5 years behind schedule Investors are questioning neoclouds' business model but Nebius says AI computing prices are rising 12 Min Ago Cambridge Analytica still haunts Zuckerberg The Cambridge Analytica scandal from nearly a decade ago continues to haunt Zuckerberg and his social media empire. New Mexico district court judge Francis Mathew imposed a $25 billion penalty on Meta today over a state data privacy case that derived from 2018 privacy revelations. The fine, revealed in a court filing, came after a jury in a Santa Fe courthouse determined that the company formally known as Facebook should be held liable for misleading New Mexico residents about its data handling practices and methods to prevent harmful information from spreading on its family of apps. Although New Mexico was awarded $219.5 billion, based on the social media company committing over 43 million violations of the state's unfair practices act, the judge reduced that figure to $25 billion. "Facebook did not conduct the comprehensive investigation that it promised" following the Cambridge Analytica revelations, judge Mathew wrote in the filing, regarding the company's then pledge to examine the "data misuse." — Jonathan Vanian 54 Min Ago What analyst expect with Meta's Muse and AI agents Muse signage during a preview event ahead of Meta Connect in Menlo Park, California, US, on Tuesday, Sept. 22, 2026. David Paul Morris | Bloomberg | Getty Images Analysts at Bank of America wrote in a note published Friday that they expect Meta to post a sales beat, with revenue of $63.8 billion, based in part on the firm's "solid ad checks" with brands and companies that helps determine the health of the digital ad market. The analysts don't expect Muse to contribute significantly to Meta's overall business for the rest of this year and 2027 and instead "will consume capacity w/o near-term revs.," meaning that the company's AI agent efforts will take some time to grow into something bigger. Morgan Stanley analysts agree that Meta's Muse AI agent initiatives won't generate big sales anytime soon, and while they said in a Sunday research note that they are "bullish," they "encourage investors to keep reasonable adoption rates in perspective." The analysts explained that it takes a long time for new technology habits and behaviors to normalize. In 2000, when the e-commerce boom was just five years deep, for instance, the analysts noted that online retail "only made up 4% of adj retail sales" while adding that "even ~30 years in ('26) it's still only 28%." — Jonathan Vanian 2 Hours Ago Meta sets the stage for hyperscaler earnings watch now VIDEO 4:39 04:39 AI capex cycle has 2-3 more years to run, says economist Access Middle East Meta will be the first hyperscaler to reveal quarterly financials during this tech earnings cycle, with Alphabet , Microsoft and Amazon slated to report next week. The four companies combined have called for roughly $730 billion in capital expenditures this year as they stock up on graphics processing units and AI systems and look to build massive data centers around the globe . Analysts polled by FactSet expect that number to hit around $1 trillion next year, led by Alphabet, which is projected to spend over $310 billion. The stepped up spending comes as interest rates soar and concerns intensify that AI revenue won't justify the costs. Alphabet and Microsoft are scheduled to report earnings next Wednesday, followed by Amazon on Thursday. — Jonathan Vanian 3 Hours Ago Meta’s legal headaches and state AG settlement watch now VIDEO 12:01 12:01 Watch CNBC's full interview with California AG Rob Bonta Squawk on the Street Meta's past quarter wasn't all AI agents and good vibes. The social media giant agreed in August to pay nearly $17 billion to settle a major lawsuit involving a group of state attorneys general, including California's Rob Bonta. The trial centered around allegations that Meta misled the public about the true scope of child mental health related harms caused by certain design elements of apps like Facebook and Instagram , including recommendation algorithms. Meta's state AG settlement could cause the company to miss on third-quarter earnings per share due to the related $10 billion legal charge that "the street has not yet accounted for," Wolfe Research analysts wrote in a Monday note. The company still faces numerous personal injury claims and a separate federal case involving a group of nationwide school districts that also focus on allegations that apps like Instagram have had detrimental effects on the well being of children. — Jonathan Vanian

headlines.summary: General Motors is targeting a roughly two-year vehicle development cycle as it expands its use of artificial intelligence, simulation and vehicle software.
headlines.article_text: GM aims to shorten vehicle development time with AI, software push Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points General Motors is hoping to reduce the time it takes to develop vehicles, targeting a roughly two-year cycle as it expands its use of artificial intelligence, simulation and vehicle software. GM says it is using artificial intelligence, simulation and more concurrent engineering to shorten development and reduce physical testing. The automaker is also expanding in-vehicle AI and plans to introduce eyes-off highway driving beginning with the Cadillac Escalade IQ in 2028. In this article GM Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Mary Barra, chairman and chief executive officer of General Motors Co., speaks during the grand opening of General Motors global headquarters at Hudson's Detroit in Detroit, Michigan, US, on Monday, Jan. 12, 2026. Jeff Kowalsky | Bloomberg | Getty Images NEW YORK — General Motors plans to lean into artificial intelligence and vehicle software for future growth and development amid increasing competition abroad from Chinese automakers and a tougher U.S. market. The Detroit automaker on Wednesday shared new details about a proprietary AI agent it's releasing under its OnStar brand, plans for a fourth generation of more efficient all-electric vehicles and a target to cut its vehicle development time in half. GM also reconfirmed that by 2028 , it wants to have eyes-off highway driving, or "personal autonomy," that will let drivers take their attention off the road. The automaker said that technology would start with the Cadillac Escalade IQ EV before rolling out to other, more high-volume models. "All of these developments are building us the car of the future," CEO Mary Barra said Wednesday during an event laying out the plans, called "GM Forward," in downtown Manhattan. The initiatives, which Barra, Chief Product Officer Sterling Anderson and other executives discussed at the event, are designed to streamline the automaker's operations, while also improving the capabilities of its vehicles for customers. "Over the last 12 months, we've evolved how we design, engineer and build our vehicles," said Anderson, who led the event and who has been tasked with overseeing GM's latest technology transformation. GM said it is now targeting a vehicle development time of roughly two years from concept to production versus a traditional four- to five-year cycle. However, the company did not detail a timeline for reaching that goal. Read more CNBC auto news Tesla unveils long-delayed Roadster developed with SpaceX, fueling merger speculation Porsche reveals Mission S concept car that previews new design identity How lower fuel economy targets could boost pickups and V-8 engines Stellantis CEO urges incentives for carmakers who build in Europe as Chinese rivals gain ground The event comes as Chinese automakers are growing outside of the U.S. with rapid development times of new technologies and vehicles. Consulting firm AlixPartners said it believes China is currently bringing vehicles to market twice as fast as traditional automakers, with 40% to 50% less investment and a 30% cost advantage. GM also continues to play catch-up to U.S. EV leader Tesla when it comes to delivering technology advancements through over-the-air updates and automated driving capabilities . Next-generation vehicles GM said Wednesday it has major plans for its next generation of EVs and traditional vehicles with internal combustion engines. The company said those coming vehicles – regardless of type — will have 40 times the computing power and up to 50% faster cellular connectivity than prior systems. That computing power is expected to help the automaker with over-the-air updates, onboard diagnostics and AI, as well as other technologies such as automated driving features. The new brain of the vehicle will launch on the $130,000 Cadillac Escalade IQ EV in 2028 before rolling out to other models, including its next generation of EVs. GM said the forthcoming EVs are expected to be 25% more aerodynamic and 15% lighter and feature electric motors and battery packs that are more compact. AI development GM expects to achieve such targets through the use of AI in research and development. The company said it is developing a "new operating approach for vehicle development" that leans into enterprise AI and virtualization to increase speed. "This concurrent engineering model allows us to innovate faster, improve continuously, and scale new technologies across our lineup with incredible agility," the company said in a release. General Motors CEO Mary Barra (left), Chief Product Officer Sterling Anderson and President Mark Reuss at the company's GM Forward event in downtown Manhattan on Oct. 21, 2026. Michael Wayland | CNBC GM used the development of its next-generation vehicles, including a new battery chemistry, as an example of how the new technologies are reshaping its vehicle development. The company said it virtually tested more than 300,000 battery designs using its recently announced lithium manganese rich battery chemistry, or LMR, before building a single physical prototype. Anderson said Wednesday that LMR will be the exclusive battery tech for its fourth-generation EVs. GM had previously said it wanted to use those batteries in full-size electric vehicles such as its Chevrolet Silverado and Escalade IQ beginning in 2028. Anderson said GM is uniquely positioned to use AI compared to other automotive companies because of its more than 100 years in the industry as well as 30 years of OnStar. "In the age of AI, data is currency," Anderson said. "For decades, GM's engineering, manufacturing and product teams have generated unparalleled body of data that we're now using to build industry-leading AI tools." In-vehicle AI The company is building on its internal use of AI to better shape its experiences for customers. GM on Wednesday reconfirmed that it plans to launch a proprietary in-vehicle AI assistant through its OnStar technology brand. The OnStar AI assistant is expected to launch in the coming months on the 2027 Cadillac Lyriq EV through an over-the-air update before expanding to other models. GM currently uses Google's Gemini for its in-vehicle AI assistant. The company told CNBC earlier this year that the GM-developed AI will be more integrated with the vehicle. The goal for OnStar AI, which will be available through a subscription, is to help customers be productive while in the car, especially if the vehicle has self-driving capabilities that don't require the driver or passengers to monitor the system. GM on Wednesday also reiterated its plans to launch eyes-off highway driving in 2028. The automaker said a year ago that it wanted to launch that technology. It's been five years since Barra said she expected the automaker to offer personal autonomous vehicles this decade. "Our vision is that eventually every vehicle should drive itself or its occupants anywhere, and we're investing across the self-driving stack to make that real," Anderson said. In this article META Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg attends the annual Allen and Co. Sun Valley Media and Technology Conference at the Sun Valley Resort in Sun Valley, Idaho, U.S., July 9, 2026. Brendan McDermid | Reuters Meta was ordered to pay $25 billion in penalties by a New Mexico court on Wednesday as part of a data privacy case that stemmed from the company's Cambridge Analytica scandal from nearly a decade ago. The penalty, revealed in a court filing, comes after a jury in a Santa Fe courthouse found in September the social media giant liable for misleading state citizens about how it safeguards and collects user data and prevents harmful information from flourishing on its services. Although the jury concluded that Meta had over 43 million violations of the state's unfair practices act, with each transgression carrying a civil penalty as high as $5,000, a New Mexico judge was responsible for determining the ultimate fine. The Wednesday filing showed that the state was awarded $219.5 billion, but the penalty was ultimately reduced to $25 billion. "The extraordinary number of willful violations found by the jury, the duration and repetition of the conduct, the breadth of subjects on which violations occurred, the involvement of senior Facebook leadership, the size of New Mexico audiences reached, and the clear intentional and systematic nature of Facebook's repeated misstatements established in the trial record support the highest level of penalty allowed by the New Mexico Unfair Practices Act - $5,000 per violation found by the jury," New Mexico district court judge Francis Mathew wrote in the filing. The judge added that interest on the penalty shall accrue at the rate of 15% each year until the fine is paid off in full. CNBC has reached out to Meta for comment on the penalty order. Meta previously resolved various Cambridge Analytica-derived data privacy lawsuits across the nation as part of an overarching August settlement of nearly $17 billion with a coalition of state attorneys general in a separate federal case related to child safety and mental health. But because New Mexico was not part of the settlement, the state's data privacy case that arose from Meta's Cambridge Analytica scandal proceeded to trial in September. In 2022, the social media giant agreed to pay $725 million to settle a class action lawsuit that also sprang from the company's Cambridge Analytica scandal that kicked off in 2018. That scandal rocked the Mark Zuckerberg-led company before its official name change to Meta, and focused on allegations that the political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica improperly accessed the information of 87 million users , raising questions about Facebook's data handling practices. Judge Mathew said in the filing that "Facebook did not conduct the comprehensive investigation that it promised" following the Cambridge Analytica revelations. "Pressure from senior executives to keep costs down, lack of adequate enforcement resources, inadequate investigative techniques, and a desire not to create precedent for future investigations," all contributed to what the judge characterized as a "willfully ineffective" internal examination by Facebook, the filing said. Former New Mexico state Attorney General Hector Balderas originally filed the state's Cambridge Analytica-related lawsuit in 2021, while current AG Raúl Torrez oversaw the related trial. Torrez also led his state's child-safety related trial against Meta that resulted in a March jury ruling that the social media company should pay $375 million for violating the state's unfair practices act. A New Mexico judge would later order Meta to pay $567 million into an abatement fund as part of a second phase of the case that determined the social media firm's actions created a public nuisance. Meta said it disagreed with that New Mexico ruling and planned to appeal. headlines.article_text: Intel hits construction milestone at delayed Ohio chip fab Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Intel’s first Ohio fab was originally expected to begin production in 2025. Operations are now targeted for 2030 or 2031. Intel says construction and tool installation are underway at its next Arizona fab, with operations expected by the end of 2028. Reported discussions with SK Hynix could bring memory production to the Ohio site, but no deal has been confirmed. In this article INTC Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Intel announced on Oct. 21, 2026, that crews have installed the first major structural truss at its new chip fabrication plant in New Albany, Ohio. Courtesy: Intel Intel has hit a milestone in the construction of its massive chip fabrication plant in New Albany, Ohio, that's running at least five years behind schedule, a delay that's coincided with soaring demand for advanced chips. On Wednesday, Intel announced that crews have installed the first major structural truss in Ohio, which means the next part of the construction has finally begun. "This represents another significant step toward expanded U.S. leading-edge semiconductor capacity," Intel Foundry head Naga Chandrasekaran wrote in a post on the company's website on Wednesday. Intel still needs customers to make the investment pay off. In September, reports surfaced that the world's leading maker of high-bandwidth memory, SK Hynix , could team up with Intel in Ohio to lease some foundry space to make memory chips at the new site. Neither company would confirm any plans. When Intel first announced the Ohio factory in 2022, it was expected to start delivering chips in 2025. Intel pushed back that timeline, now aiming to finish construction in 2030. A second Ohio fab is also planned for completion in 2031 at the site, just northeast of Columbus. The delay reflects a broader recalibration of Intel's foundry ambitions under CEO Lip-Bu Tan. The Ohio factory is only one piece of Intel's ambitious build-out to start making chips for outside customers that began under former CEO Pat Gelsinger. When Tan took the helm in 2025, his turnaround strategy was more cautious, choosing to wait for customer demand before forging ahead with ambitious chip fab plans. Still, by late 2025, Intel was in high-volume production at its Arizona chip fab , producing its most advanced 18A chips. On Wednesday, Chandrasekaran also announced that operations at its next fab in Arizona are expected to begin by the end of 2028. But Intel has yet to land a major external customer for those 18A chips coming out of Arizona. Instead, Intel is using them to make its own processors for devices. Once a dominant force in the chip manufacturing landscape, Intel hit major delays with its 7- and 10-nanometer nodes, triggering the stock's worst year ever in 2024. Customers have been reluctant to commit again since. Now, Intel's window of opportunity may have arrived alongside record demand for AI, as leading chip manufacturer Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. can't make chips fast enough. Even for the biggest chipmakers like Nvidia , Advanced Micro Devices , Apple and Broadcom , "competition is extremely fierce," to get space on TSMC's factory lines, according to Mizuho Securities analyst Jordan Klein. Intel could offer customers an alternative source for chip production, according to TechInsights analyst Dan Hutcheson. "People want a second source to be able to twist TSMC's arm and keep them honest on pricing," Hutcheson said. "All the big ones have been testing there." headlines.title: Stocks making the biggest moves midday: SpaceX, Meta Platforms, Super Micro Computer, Roivant Sciences & more
headlines.summary: Here are some of the companies making headlines in midday trading.
headlines.article_text: Stocks making the biggest moves midday: SPCX, META, SMCI, ROIV Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Here are some of the companies making headlines in midday trading. Roivant Sciences — Shares rose more than 4% after the company's immune-modifying pill Lisraya reached its primary efficacy goals in two Phase 3 trials for non-infectious uveitis, a disease of the eye. Bloom Energy — The fuel cell company jumped more than 6% as traders snapped up shares ahead of Thursday's third-quarter report. The FactSet consensus sees earnings coming in at 69 cents per share on revenue of $1.07 billion. Wolfe Research dubbed the company a "recent outperformer" in its preview of clean energy earnings, saying "demand signal continues to build, beat and raise potential." Bitcoin-linked stocks — Bitcoin jumped more than 2% to trade above $84,000 as investors flocked to risk assets. A raft of crypto-related stocks leapt alongside it, with Strategy gaining 7% and bitcoin miner MARA Holdings rising more than 3%. Riot Platforms advanced 2%. Alphabet — Shares of the tech giant slipped 2% after OpenAI said that its models will be available for developers via Google's cloud. The move follows years of competition between OpenAI and Alphabet, and it means the ChatGPT maker will have its models available on all three of the major U.S. cloud companies. Meta Platforms — The social media giant jumped 2% ahead of quarterly results due after the bell Wednesday. Muse, the company's artificial intelligence model, will likely be a key focal point after its closely watched rollout this fall. SpaceX — Shares gained 10% after the Elon Musk-led rocket company reported a 161% jump in third-quarter revenue to $14.58 billion. Musk also said that SpaceX and Tesla , his automaker, have formed special committees to discuss a potential merger. Tesla shares were up 3%. Telecom company EchoStar , which owns a stake in SpaceX, saw shares rise 8%. Space stocks — Other aerospace companies were higher following SpaceX's earnings jump. Rocket Lab rose 4%, while Firefly Aerospace jumped 5%. Netflix — Shares of Netflix fell almost 5% after the streaming giant narrowed its 2026 full-year forecast . The streaming giant now sees revenue at $51.1 billion, reflecting a 13% year-over-year increase and landing at the low-end of its earlier guidance range of $51 billion to $51.4 billion. AT & T — The telecommunications company slid 6% despite reporting an earnings and revenue beat in its third-quarter financial report. AT & T also hiked its full-year earnings guidance, though it reiterated capital expenditures that came in slightly above expectations, according to FactSet. Capital One Financial — The lender and credit card issuer gained about 4%. Third-quarter net income reached $3.5 billion, or $5.61 per share, up from $3.2 billion, or $4.83 a share in the year-earlier period. United Airlines — The Chicago-based carrier jumped 5%. While third-quarter results missed on the top and bottom lines, the company pointed out that passengers are still booking even as fares have risen. Passenger counts are up more than 2% from the year-ago period, while domestic passenger unit revenue gained 14.5% in that timeframe. Super Micro Computer — Shares rallied 9% after the data center server company hiked its fiscal first-quarter revenue outlook. Super Micro sees revenue for the period between $18.5 billion and $19.5 billion, up from a previous range of $14.5 billion to $15.5 billion. Dell Technologies , Hewlett Packard Enterprise — Super Micro's server competitors Dell and HPE were also higher on the news of the company's guidance update. Dell jumped almost 5%, while HPE rose 3%. Danaher — Shares lost 3% after the life sciences and diagnostics innovator reported a slight revenue miss in its third-quarter earnings report. Revenue came in at $6.55 billion, compared the $6.56 billion FactSet consensus estimate. Adjusted earnings, however, beat estimates, and the company raised its full-year guidance for the metric. — CNBC's Nick Wells, Darla Mercado, Deena Zaidi, Fred Imbert and Scott Schnipper contributed reporting.
